newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy offers 700 million shares in ENI.
newsitem.headline: Italy offers 700 million shares in ENI.

text.p: The Italian Treasury said on Sunday that it was offering a total of 700 million ordinary shares in the second tranche of the sale of state energy group ENI, the country's largest publicly traded company.
A Treasury statement said a minimum of 250 million of the ordinary shares would be offered in a public sale offer (OPV) of which up to 25 percent was destined for ENI employees.
Shares in the OPV will be sold at a discount to the market rate and the price is to be announced on October 20, the day before the second flotation is launched.
The Treasury said additional shares may also be offered under a "green shoe" arrangement, which allows institutional investors to receive additional stock to that already on offer.
This would be up to a maximum of 15 percent of the global offer, or 105 million shares, the Treasury said.
More details of the second tranche sale, equivalent to about nine percent of ENI stock, are due to be announced at a Treasury news conference on Monday.
Last November, the Treasury sold a first 15 percent tranche of ENI, which has a market capitalisation of some $35 billion.

It was floated at 5,250 lire to trade in Milan, London and New York and brought 6.3 trillion lire ($4.0 billion) into the state coffers. ENI shares closed trade on Friday in Milan 3.02 percent up at 7,302 lire after a year's high of 7,925 lire.
The government has indicated it might use the proceeds from the second tranche sale to reduce Italy's budget deficit rather than state debt.
The Treasury, which will retain control of ENI, has not indicated its plans for further sell-offs of the energy group.
A series of world-wide road shows start on Monday and the Italian public sale runs from October 21 to 25. The share price will be fixed on October 26 and trading is expected to start on October 29.

A first tranche sale of Enel, the world's second-largest electricity group after EDF of France, is due to take place some time in 1997 after the privatisation of state telecoms group Stet, slated for next spring.
The sell-off of Enel should have begun late last year but the operation was put off by a government crisis and lack of a sector regulating authority. The watchdog has now been created.
Enel Managing Director Franco Tato told a weekend conference on the liberalisation of public services that privatisation meant the state selling 51 percent of a company's shares.
"As long as the state holds on to a golden share there can't be a real separation. Either you privatise the whole of a company or you don't call it a privatisation," he said.

The Anglo-Saxon concept of the golden share allows the state to continue to exercise particular powers in a privatised public company, including the right to name the chairman and being able to veto mergers or the entry of new shareholders.
The concept was adopted into Italian law in 1994 and was used for the first time with the ENI sale last November.
For Enel, it remains unclear whether the state intends to hold a golden share. $=1,520 lire
